title: Ibrahim, an example
hook: in Ibrahim and those with him is an excellent example (60:4)
tomorrow: Kindness to those who don't fight you

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Surah Al-Hashr with the names at the end, and your line was his are the beautiful names. Which name fit a moment in your day? Today, Surah sixty, She who is Tested. Day six hundred twenty-two.

Most people have one person they quietly copy. A grandmother who always set an extra plate. A teacher who answered every question as if it were a good one. You catch yourself doing what they did, years later, without deciding to. The Qur'an gives the phrase an excellent example to very few. One is the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in Surah Al-Ahzab. The other is Ibrahim, Abraham, the friend of God, with those who stood beside him. And when Surah sixty names him, it holds up two sides of him at once.

Verse four. Pickthall: "There is a goodly pattern for you in Abraham and those with him". The Arabic is uswa hasana, an excellent example, a pattern to follow. It's the same phrase Surah Al-Ahzab uses for the Prophet. Then the verse says what the pattern is. Ibrahim and those with him told their own people, plainly, that they would not worship what their people worshipped besides God. They stood firm, even against their own families. That firmness is one side. The surah, named for a woman who is tested, was revealed at a time of divided loyalties, and it speaks to people torn between faith and family. But the very same verse sets one thing apart: Ibrahim's words to his father, I will ask forgiveness for you, though I have no power to do anything for you against God. Many classical commentators read that as the one part of the pattern not to copy, since Surah At-Tawbah says Ibrahim later stopped asking forgiveness for his father. Still, the way he spoke is remembered. Even while parting ways, Ibrahim spoke to his father with tenderness. Surah Maryam remembers the same moment: Ibrahim says to his father, peace be upon you, I will ask my Lord to forgive you. Firm in belief, gentle in speech. That's the second side. And there's a third side people loved to copy: his table. In Surah Adh-Dhariyat, strangers arrive at Ibrahim's door. He doesn't know who they are. He hurries off to his family and comes back with a fattened calf. Ibrahim's hospitality became a byword. Firm about what he believed, soft toward the father he disagreed with, and quick to feed a stranger. The verse calls the whole pattern beautiful.
screen: `USWA HASANA: AN EXCELLENT EXAMPLE.` · `FIRM WITH HIS PEOPLE.` · `TENDER WITH HIS FATHER.` · `A FATTENED CALF FOR STRANGERS.`

segments.voice: The practice: follow one of his habits: hospitality. Sit, and breathe. Picture your own door, or your desk, or your table. Who might come to it this week: a neighbor, a new colleague, a friend you've lost touch with? Picture Ibrahim hurrying to bring the best he had. Choose one small act of welcome you could offer: a cup of tea, a seat, a meal, a warm hello. Hold it in mind. The bell holds the time.
Ibrahim. In him and those with him, Surah sixty says, is an excellent example: firm in faith, tender with his father, and generous at his table. Today's word.
Your line: an excellent example. Today, offer your one act of welcome, and offer it quickly, the way Ibrahim hurried. Day six hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: Muslims honor Ibrahim as the friend of God, khalil Allah, and invoke him in every prayer; his hospitality is held up as a model, and Muslim hosts often speak of honoring the guest as a duty of faith.

original.note: Arabic: an excellent example, a beautiful pattern. Used for Ibrahim (60:4, 60:6) and the Prophet (33:21).

trapdoor: what you thought: Ibrahim is an example because he was a great prophet.
what it means: an example of firmness, tenderness and hospitality, all in one person.
what a scholar hears: uswa hasana in 60:4 and 33:21; the exception for Ibrahim's istighfar for his father, read with 19:47 and 9:114; the guests of 51:24–27.

sources.quoted: There is a goodly pattern for you in Abraham and those with him

sources.ref: Qur'an 33:21 (an excellent example in the Messenger)
Qur'an 19:47 (peace be upon you, I will ask forgiveness for you)
Qur'an 51:24–27 (Ibrahim's guests and the fattened calf)

notes: Pickthall wording of 60:4 quoted from memory; please confirm.

60:4 also includes strong words of enmity toward idol worship 'until ye believe in Allah only'; the script summarizes it as Ibrahim telling his people he would not worship what they worshipped. A Keeper may want to adjust.
The claim that uswa hasana is used only for Ibrahim (60:4, 60:6) and the Prophet (33:21) should be confirmed.

Reviewer fix: the earlier draft presented the 60:4 exception (Ibrahim's promise to seek forgiveness for his father) as part of the example to admire. Most classical commentators (e.g. Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari) read it as excluded from the example, read with 9:114. The teach now says so; the tenderness of his speech is drawn from 19:47. Confirm the framing.
